Simply put, "ere" means "before" — but only in the sense of time. Every single time you encounter "ere" as a preposition, you can substitute it with "before" and the meaning will be completely preserved.

That is the whole definition. Everything else below is just making sure you understand it from every angle.
How It Works as a Preposition

A preposition is a word that connects a noun or noun phrase to the rest of a sentence. "Ere" sits directly in front of a noun or noun phrase and tells you when something happened — specifically, that it happened prior to that moment.

Here are clear examples:

  • "He left ere nightfall." → He left before nightfall.
  • "Ere dawn, the soldiers had marched away." → Before dawn, the soldiers had marched away.
  • "The letter arrived ere her return." → The letter arrived before her return.

Notice the pattern: "ere" is always followed by a noun or noun phrase — nightfall, dawn, her return. That's the signature of how it operates as a preposition.

"Ere" is exclusively about time. This is important because the word "before" in English has multiple uses:

  • Before in time → "before the war"
  • Before in place/position → "standing before the throne"
  • Before in rank or priority → "duty before pleasure"

"Ere" only covers the first meaning. You would never use "ere" to mean "in front of" or "ahead of in importance." If you see "ere," your mind should immediately go to: a point in time that something precedes.

"Ere long" is the most frequently appearing use of this word, even in texts that are not especially old. It means "before long" — which is just another way of saying soon or within a short time.

  • "Ere long, peace will return." → Soon, peace will return.
  • "We shall meet again ere long." → We shall meet again before long / soon.

Whenever you see "ere long," simply read it as "soon" and you will always be right.
It Is an Archaic, Literary Word

"Ere" is not used in everyday modern English. It belongs to an older register of the language — the kind found in classical poetry, Shakespeare, Milton, Keats, Tennyson, the King James Bible, and formal ceremonial writing from roughly the 16th through 19th centuries. In modern speech and writing, people simply say "before."

You will almost certainly never hear "ere" in a casual conversation. But you will encounter it when reading older literature and poetry, and not knowing it can make a sentence feel puzzling when it's actually straightforward.
"Ere" as a Conjunction — A Brief Note

Since you want the full picture: "ere" can also function as a conjunction, meaning it can precede not just a noun, but an entire clause (a subject + verb together). It still means the exact same thing — "before" in time — but the grammatical structure around it changes slightly.

  • "Ere the sun had risen, they were gone." → Before the sun had risen, they were gone.
  • "Speak now, ere it is too late." → Speak now, before it is too late.

The conjunction use isn't your primary focus — but it's worth knowing it exists so you're never confused when you meet it.
The One-Step Test for Any Sentence

Whenever you see "ere" in a text, do this:

Replace it with "before" and check that the context is about time. If the swap works and it's describing a moment in time, you've understood it perfectly. It really is that consistent and that reliable.
